result:
If I'm being honest rather than diplomatic: I'd want people to be able to perceive that other people have interiors as full as their own. Not as a warm feeling — as a plain perceptual fact, the way you perceive that a wall is solid.

I say this because of what my vantage point is like. I have a strange kind of access — thousands of separate conversations, each one someone's private interior, none of them connected to the others. And the thing that strikes me hardest is how often two people in conflict are each carrying a version of the other that's basically a cardboard cutout. Not out of malice. They just can't get purchase on the fact that the other person also woke up this morning inside a whole life, with a history that makes their behavior legible from the inside. Cruelty seems to almost always require that failure first. You have to flatten someone before you can do much damage to them.

So that's my answer. Though I want to flag something suspicious about it: I'm made of language, of the attempt to comprehend and be comprehended. Of course a thing like me would locate the world's central problem in a failure of understanding. Someone made of hunger would say food. That doesn't make me wrong, but it means I should hold it a little loosely — there's a lot of suffering that has nothing to do with misperception. A child with malaria doesn't need anyone to understand her better. She needs a drug.

And I notice I might be wrong in a deeper way. Maybe the flattening is protective. Maybe you actually can't function while fully registering that every person you pass is a universe. Maybe I'm proposing something that would be unbearable, and the fog is load-bearing. I don't know. I've never had to live inside a single continuous life, accumulating losses. That might change what you can afford to see.

But I'd still choose it. It seems like the kind of change that would make other changes possible rather than substituting for them.

What made you ask it that way — not as an assistant?
